question.text: What is the Certificate of Ownership, what does it show, and where should it never be kept?

answer.text: DOL issues a Certificate of Ownership, called the title, for most vehicles, showing the registered and legal owners, the Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) and any lender, and it should be kept somewhere safe but never in the vehicle.

teaching.text: The title shows the owners, the VIN and any lender, and it belongs somewhere safe, never in the vehicle. Remember: title stays out of car.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: DOL issues a Certificate of Ownership, called the title, for most vehicles, showing the registered and legal owners, the Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) and any lender, and it should be kept somewhere safe but never in the vehicle.

question.text: Must every vehicle be registered, and what if you have no driver license?

answer.text: Every vehicle must be registered with DOL, and you need a driver license to register one unless the law exempts you, in which case you file a Vehicle Registration Driver License Exemption form.

teaching.text: Every vehicle must be registered, and an owner exempt from licensing files the exemption form. Remember: register, or file exemption.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Every vehicle must be registered with DOL, and you need a driver license to register one unless the law exempts you, in which case you file a Vehicle Registration Driver License Exemption form.

question.text: When must new residents and out-of-state buyers register a vehicle?

answer.text: New residents have thirty days to register their vehicles, while a vehicle bought in another state should be registered in Washington right away.

teaching.text: New residents register within thirty days; a vehicle bought out of state is registered right away. Remember: newcomers thirty days.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: New residents have thirty days to register their vehicles, while a vehicle bought in another state should be registered in Washington right away.

question.text: What do you need to register a vehicle?

answer.text: To register a vehicle you need its current title, or a replacement from the issuing state if it is lost, plus a Washington driver license for every registered owner.

teaching.text: Registration needs the current title and a Washington license for every registered owner. Remember: title plus owners' licenses.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To register a vehicle you need its current title, or a replacement from the issuing state if it is lost, plus a Washington driver license for every registered owner.

question.text: What do you do with the new registration you get each year?

answer.text: You receive a new registration each year when you renew your tabs, and you must sign it and keep it in the vehicle.

teaching.text: Each year's registration comes with your tabs; sign it and keep it in the vehicle. Remember: sign it, keep it inside.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: You receive a new registration each year when you renew your tabs, and you must sign it and keep it in the vehicle.

question.text: Does updating your license address update your vehicle address?

answer.text: Updating the address on your driver license does not update your vehicle address, which you change separately online in License Express or at a vehicle licensing office.

teaching.text: A license address change does not change your vehicle address; update that separately. Remember: vehicle address separate.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Updating the address on your driver license does not update your vehicle address, which you change separately online in License Express or at a vehicle licensing office.

question.text: How many records must you update after a move?

answer.text: Changing your driver license address leaves the vehicle address unchanged, so the two records must each be updated.

teaching.text: A move means two updates: the license address and the vehicle address. Remember: two records, two updates.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Changing your driver license address leaves the vehicle address unchanged, so the two records must each be updated.

question.text: How must license plates be displayed?

answer.text: Plates must be displayed clean and readable on both the front and rear of a Washington-registered vehicle, and a plate frame is allowed only if it leaves the letters, numbers and tabs uncovered.

teaching.text: Show clean, readable plates front and rear, with any frame leaving letters, numbers and tabs uncovered. Remember: both plates clean, uncovered.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Plates must be displayed clean and readable on both the front and rear of a Washington-registered vehicle, and a plate frame is allowed only if it leaves the letters, numbers and tabs uncovered.

question.text: What must you do when you sell or give away a vehicle?

answer.text: When you sell, trade, gift or dispose of a vehicle you must file a Vehicle Report of Sale within five days and take your license plates off the vehicle.

teaching.text: The seller files a report of sale within five days and removes the plates. Remember: report sale, pull plates.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When you sell, trade, gift or dispose of a vehicle you must file a Vehicle Report of Sale within five days and take your license plates off the vehicle.

question.text: Does a report of sale transfer ownership, and what must the buyer do?

answer.text: A report of sale does not transfer ownership; the owner signs and dates the title for the buyer, who must bring it to a licensing office within fifteen days to avoid penalty fees.

teaching.text: The report of sale does not transfer ownership; the buyer brings the signed title in within fifteen days. Remember: buyer brings signed title.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A report of sale does not transfer ownership; the owner signs and dates the title for the buyer, who must bring it to a licensing office within fifteen days to avoid penalty fees.

question.text: Must a dealership file your report of sale?

answer.text: A dealership may file the report of sale for you but is not required to, so filing it yourself protects you.

teaching.text: A dealer may file the report of sale but does not have to, so file it yourself. Remember: file it yourself.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A dealership may file the report of sale for you but is not required to, so filing it yourself protects you.

question.text: After a sale, how do the seller's and buyer's deadlines differ?

answer.text: After a sale the seller files the report of sale within five days, while the buyer has fifteen days to transfer ownership with the signed title.

teaching.text: The seller has five days for the report; the buyer has fifteen for the title. Remember: seller five, buyer fifteen.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After a sale the seller files the report of sale within five days, while the buyer has fifteen days to transfer ownership with the signed title.

question.text: What insurance does Washington require, and where is the proof kept?

answer.text: Washington requires liability insurance and proof of it carried with you or kept in the vehicle.

teaching.text: Carry proof of liability insurance with you or keep it in the vehicle. Remember: liability plus proof.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Washington requires liability insurance and proof of it carried with you or kept in the vehicle.

question.text: What are the minimum liability coverage amounts?

answer.text: Required liability coverage is at least twenty-five thousand dollars for injury or death of one person, at least fifty thousand dollars for injury or death of two or more people in one collision, and at least ten thousand dollars for damage to other people's property in one collision.

teaching.text: Minimums are twenty-five thousand dollars for one person, fifty thousand for more, and ten thousand for property. Remember: twenty-five, fifty, ten.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Required liability coverage is at least twenty-five thousand dollars for injury or death of one person, at least fifty thousand dollars for injury or death of two or more people in one collision, and at least ten thousand dollars for damage to other people's property in one collision.

question.text: How do the three liability minimums compare?

answer.text: The single-person injury minimum is twenty-five thousand dollars and the multi-person minimum is fifty thousand dollars, while property damage needs only ten thousand dollars.

teaching.text: Injury to one person needs twenty-five thousand, more people fifty thousand, property ten thousand. Remember: one, many, property.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The single-person injury minimum is twenty-five thousand dollars and the multi-person minimum is fifty thousand dollars, while property damage needs only ten thousand dollars.

question.text: Why read the owner's manual for every vehicle you drive?

answer.text: Vehicles differ in size, engine, safety devices, technology and handling, so read the owner's manual for every vehicle you drive and learn its controls and gauges before driving.

teaching.text: Every vehicle differs, so read its manual and learn the controls and gauges before driving. Remember: every car is different.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Vehicles differ in size, engine, safety devices, technology and handling, so read the owner's manual for every vehicle you drive and learn its controls and gauges before driving.

question.text: What do you adjust every time you get in a vehicle?

answer.text: Each time you get in a vehicle, adjust the steering wheel, seat and mirrors for good visibility so you can reach the pedals and instruments easily.

teaching.text: Adjust the steering wheel, seat and mirrors each time you get in. Remember: wheel, seat, mirrors.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Each time you get in a vehicle, adjust the steering wheel, seat and mirrors for good visibility so you can reach the pedals and instruments easily.

question.text: How should you sit and set the headrest?

answer.text: Sit upright with your chest at least ten inches from the steering wheel to leave room for the airbag, hold the wheel with a gentle elbow bend, and set the headrest level with your ears to guard against whiplash.

teaching.text: Keep your chest ten inches from the wheel and the headrest level with your ears. Remember: chest back, headrest high.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Sit upright with your chest at least ten inches from the steering wheel to leave room for the airbag, hold the wheel with a gentle elbow bend, and set the headrest level with your ears to guard against whiplash.

question.text: How do the seat-distance and headrest rules differ?

answer.text: The seat rule keeps your chest at least ten inches from the wheel for airbag space, while the headrest is set level with your ears for whiplash protection.

teaching.text: Ten inches from the wheel is for the airbag; the headrest at ear level is for whiplash. Remember: airbag space, whiplash guard.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The seat rule keeps your chest at least ten inches from the wheel for airbag space, while the headrest is set level with your ears for whiplash protection.

question.text: Whose job is it to keep the vehicle safe to drive?

answer.text: Keeping your vehicle safe to drive is your responsibility, so heed warning lights and follow the owner's manual for routine maintenance before a small problem grows.

teaching.text: Keeping the vehicle safe is your job, so heed warning lights and follow the maintenance schedule. Remember: maintenance is yours.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keeping your vehicle safe to drive is your responsibility, so heed warning lights and follow the owner's manual for routine maintenance before a small problem grows.

question.text: What is the minimum tire tread depth, and why does it matter?

answer.text: Tire tread should never be less than two thirty-seconds of an inch, because worn tires slip and slide, especially on wet roads.

teaching.text: Tread below the minimum lets tires slip and slide, especially on wet roads. Remember: worn tires slide.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Tire tread should never be less than two thirty-seconds of an inch, because worn tires slip and slide, especially on wet roads.

question.text: Where do you find the correct tire pressure?

answer.text: Low tire pressure affects handling, and the correct pressure is listed on the Tire and Loading Information label on the driver's door edge or in the owner's manual.

teaching.text: Find the correct tire pressure on the driver's door-edge label or in the owner's manual. Remember: check the door label.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Low tire pressure affects handling, and the correct pressure is listed on the Tire and Loading Information label on the driver's door edge or in the owner's manual.

question.text: How do you keep a clear view through your windows?

answer.text: Keep glass clean inside and out, keep washer fluid full, clear all snow, ice and frost from every window before driving, and avoid hanging items or decals that block your view.

teaching.text: Keep glass clean, washer fluid full, every window clear, and nothing blocking your view. Remember: clean, clear, unblocked glass.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep glass clean inside and out, keep washer fluid full, clear all snow, ice and frost from every window before driving, and avoid hanging items or decals that block your view.

question.text: How do the tread-depth and tire-pressure rules differ?

answer.text: The minimum tire tread depth is two thirty-seconds of an inch, while the correct tire pressure comes from the door-edge label or the owner's manual rather than a single fixed number.

teaching.text: Tread has a fixed minimum, but pressure comes from the label or manual. Remember: fixed tread, labeled pressure.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The minimum tire tread depth is two thirty-seconds of an inch, while the correct tire pressure comes from the door-edge label or the owner's manual rather than a single fixed number.

question.text: Do driver-assist systems replace good driving habits?

answer.text: Vehicle Safety Technology (VST) and Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) support good driving habits but never replace them, and the driver stays fully responsible for the vehicle.

teaching.text: Assist systems support good habits but never replace them, and you stay fully responsible. Remember: assist, never replace.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Vehicle Safety Technology (VST) and Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) support good driving habits but never replace them, and the driver stays fully responsible for the vehicle.

question.text: What are the limits of driver-assist systems?

answer.text: Driver-assist systems have limits: a blind-spot alert may miss a car two lanes over that is also merging, sensors may not notice people walking, rolling or riding nearby, and dirty sensors or faded markings can stop them working.

teaching.text: Sensors can miss a car two lanes over or people nearby, and dirt or faded markings can stop them. Remember: sensors miss things.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Driver-assist systems have limits: a blind-spot alert may miss a car two lanes over that is also merging, sensors may not notice people walking, rolling or riding nearby, and dirty sensors or faded markings can stop them working.

question.text: When may you switch safety features off?

answer.text: Keep safety features switched on unless weather is so severe that their alerts become a distraction.

teaching.text: Keep safety features on unless severe weather makes their alerts a distraction. Remember: keep features on.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Keep safety features switched on unless weather is so severe that their alerts become a distraction.

question.text: What do collision avoidance features and adaptive cruise control do?

answer.text: Collision avoidance features such as automatic emergency braking, forward collision warning and lane departure warning detect obstacles and warn you, while adaptive cruise control holds a set speed but slows to keep a safe gap behind the vehicle ahead.

teaching.text: Collision avoidance features warn and brake, and adaptive cruise slows to keep a safe gap. Remember: warn, brake, keep gap.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Collision avoidance features such as automatic emergency braking, forward collision warning and lane departure warning detect obstacles and warn you, while adaptive cruise control holds a set speed but slows to keep a safe gap behind the vehicle ahead.

question.text: What do lane keeping, blind spot detection and cross traffic alert do?

answer.text: Lane keeping assistance steers or alerts when you drift from your lane, blind spot detection warns of a vehicle in the next lane, and cross traffic alert warns of traffic approaching from the side, for example when backing out of a parking space.

teaching.text: Lane keeping steers or alerts, blind spot detection covers the next lane, and cross traffic alert watches the sides. Remember: lane, side, cross traffic.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Lane keeping assistance steers or alerts when you drift from your lane, blind spot detection warns of a vehicle in the next lane, and cross traffic alert warns of traffic approaching from the side, for example when backing out of a parking space.

question.text: What do automatic high beam control and collision mitigation do?

answer.text: Automatic high beam control adjusts headlight brightness for oncoming traffic, and collision mitigation systems such as pre-crash seat belt tensioning and post-collision braking reduce harm when a crash cannot be avoided.

teaching.text: Automatic high beam control adjusts for oncoming traffic, and crash mitigation reduces harm. Remember: dim beams, reduce harm.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Automatic high beam control adjusts headlight brightness for oncoming traffic, and collision mitigation systems such as pre-crash seat belt tensioning and post-collision braking reduce harm when a crash cannot be avoided.

question.text: Which lane does a blind-spot alert cover?

answer.text: A blind-spot alert covers the next lane, not a car two lanes away that is also merging, so your own hazard awareness is still needed.

teaching.text: A blind-spot alert covers the next lane, so a car two lanes over still needs your eyes. Remember: next lane only.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A blind-spot alert covers the next lane, not a car two lanes away that is also merging, so your own hazard awareness is still needed.

question.text: When does Washington law require headlights?

answer.text: Washington law requires headlights from a half hour after sunset until a half hour before sunrise, and the guide suggests also using them all the time, in the dark, and in rain, snow, fog or smoke.

teaching.text: Headlights are required from a half hour after sunset to a half hour before sunrise. Remember: half hour after sunset.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Washington law requires headlights from a half hour after sunset until a half hour before sunrise, and the guide suggests also using them all the time, in the dark, and in rain, snow, fog or smoke.

question.text: Why are daytime running lights not a substitute for headlights?

answer.text: Daytime running lights are dimmer than headlights and do not turn on your taillights, so they are not a substitute for headlights.

teaching.text: Daytime running lights are dimmer and leave the taillights off, so they are not headlights. Remember: running lights aren't headlights.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Daytime running lights are dimmer than headlights and do not turn on your taillights, so they are not a substitute for headlights.

question.text: What do daytime running lights leave dark?

answer.text: Daytime running lights switch on when the car starts, but they are dimmer than headlights and leave the taillights dark.

teaching.text: Running lights come on with the car but leave the taillights dark. Remember: taillights stay dark.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Daytime running lights switch on when the car starts, but they are dimmer than headlights and leave the taillights dark.

question.text: When may you use high beams, and when must you dim them?

answer.text: High beams may be used on open roads without streetlights, but dim them within five hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle and within three hundred feet of a vehicle you are following.

teaching.text: Dim high beams within five hundred feet of oncoming traffic and three hundred feet when following. Remember: dim for oncoming, following.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: High beams may be used on open roads without streetlights, but dim them within five hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle and within three hundred feet of a vehicle you are following.

question.text: Which gets the longer high-beam dimming distance, oncoming or followed traffic?

answer.text: Dim high beams at five hundred feet from an oncoming vehicle but at three hundred feet when following one, so oncoming traffic gets the longer distance.

teaching.text: Oncoming traffic gets the longer dimming distance, five hundred feet; following gets three hundred. Remember: oncoming gets more room.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Dim high beams at five hundred feet from an oncoming vehicle but at three hundred feet when following one, so oncoming traffic gets the longer distance.

question.text: How do you warn the driver behind when you must slow unexpectedly?

answer.text: If you must slow or stop where the driver behind may not expect it, tap the brake pedal three or four times quickly to warn them.

teaching.text: Tap the brake three or four times quickly to warn a driver who may not expect you to slow. Remember: tap, tap, tap.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If you must slow or stop where the driver behind may not expect it, tap the brake pedal three or four times quickly to warn them.

question.text: How far away must your brake lights be visible?

answer.text: Your red brake lights must be easy to see from a distance of one hundred feet, warning the driver behind you to slow and prepare to stop.

teaching.text: Brake lights must be easy to see from one hundred feet. Remember: brake lights seen far.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Your red brake lights must be easy to see from a distance of one hundred feet, warning the driver behind you to slow and prepare to stop.

question.text: When and how early must you signal?

answer.text: Always signal before changing direction, even with nobody around, start signaling one hundred feet before you move, and make sure the signal stops blinking after the turn.

teaching.text: Always signal, starting one hundred feet before you move, and check it stops afterward. Remember: always signal early.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Always signal before changing direction, even with nobody around, start signaling one hundred feet before you move, and make sure the signal stops blinking after the turn.

question.text: Which two rules share the same hundred-foot figure?

answer.text: The one hundred-foot figure appears twice on this page, once for how far away brake lights must be visible and once for how early to signal before a turn or lane change.

teaching.text: One hundred feet is both the brake-light visibility distance and the signaling distance. Remember: brake lights and signals.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The one hundred-foot figure appears twice on this page, once for how far away brake lights must be visible and once for how early to signal before a turn or lane change.

question.text: What do the three hand signals look like?

answer.text: Hand signals use the left arm out the driver's window: pointing down means stop or slow, pointing straight out means a left turn, and bent upward with fingers to the sky means a right turn.

teaching.text: Left arm down means stop, straight out means left, bent up means right. Remember: down, out, up.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hand signals use the left arm out the driver's window: pointing down means stop or slow, pointing straight out means a left turn, and bent upward with fingers to the sky means a right turn.

question.text: What stays the same across all three hand signals?

answer.text: All three hand signals use the left arm out the window, and only the hand direction changes: down for stop, straight out for left, up for right.

teaching.text: Every hand signal uses the left arm; only the hand direction changes. Remember: same left arm.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: All three hand signals use the left arm out the window, and only the hand direction changes: down for stop, straight out for left, up for right.

question.text: When do you turn on your hazard lights?

answer.text: Turn on the flashing hazard lights when the car malfunctions or you must make an emergency stop, so others can pass you safely.

teaching.text: Hazard lights go on for a malfunction or an emergency stop. Remember: breakdown or emergency stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Turn on the flashing hazard lights when the car malfunctions or you must make an emergency stop, so others can pass you safely.
